blocks.content: Topology spread constraints offer a more flexible, fine-grained way to distribute Pods evenly across a cluster than the more binary spread-or-don't behavior of pod anti-affinity.
1. Even Distribution, as the Actual Goal
blocks.text: 1. Even Distribution, as the Actual Goal

blocks.content: Where anti-affinity expresses "keep these Pods apart" as a constraint, topology spread constraints directly express the actual goal: even distribution of matching Pods across a given topology domain, nodes, zones, or any other topology key.

blocks.alt: The actual goal, even distribution, expressed directly rather than indirectly

blocks.content:
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: my-app

codes.yaml:
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: my-app

blocks.content: 2. maxSkew Controls How Uneven It Can Get
blocks.text: 2. maxSkew Controls How Uneven It Can Get

blocks.content: maxSkew is the key tuning knob, it caps the maximum allowed difference in matching Pod count between any two topology domains, a maxSkew of 1 means no zone can have more than one extra matching Pod compared to the least-loaded zone.

blocks.alt: A precise, numeric cap on exactly how imbalanced distribution is allowed to get

blocks.content: Anti-affinity is fundamentally more binary, spread these Pods apart, or don't, topology spread constraints give you fine-grained, numeric control over exactly how much imbalance is acceptable, a genuinely more expressive tool for this specific goal.

blocks.alt: Fine-grained numeric control, instead of a binary spread-or-not decision

blocks.content: 4. Deciding What Happens if It Cannot Be Satisfied
blocks.text: 4. Deciding What Happens if It Cannot Be Satisfied

blocks.content: whenUnsatisfiable controls the fallback behavior, DoNotSchedule treats the constraint as a hard requirement (the Pod simply will not be scheduled if it cannot be satisfied), ScheduleAnyway treats it as a soft, best-effort preference instead.

blocks.alt: A choice between a hard requirement and a soft, best-effort attempt

blocks.content: A production Deployment spreading its replicas evenly across availability zones, with a tight maxSkew and DoNotSchedule, is a realistic, common pattern for genuinely robust high availability.

blocks.alt: Replicas spread evenly across zones, with a strict, enforced balance

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Topology spread constraints directly express even distribution as the goal, with maxSkew giving precise, numeric control over how much imbalance is tolerated.
They offer more fine-grained control than the more binary pod anti-affinity, and whenUnsatisfiable decides whether the constraint is a hard requirement or a soft preference.
